grounded_facts: Troy, handcuffed behind his back, cannot access his breathing valve and begins to suffocate; a soldier cuts his cuffs, allowing him to breathe.
memories.memory_text: I watched Troy struggle on the ground, unable to reach his breathing valve because his hands were cuffed behind him, and then a soldier stepped in, cut the cuffs with a knife, and Troy finally managed to turn his valve and breathe.

grounded_facts: Archie reveals the presence of stolen Kuwaiti gold to General Horn, who verifies it and shifts his stance on the situation.
memories.memory_text: I saw the MP knock over the barrel and spill the gold bars onto the sand, and I watched General Horn look it over, realizing he was shifting his stance once he saw what we had.

grounded_facts: Archie reveals the gold and appeals to General Horn's sense of honor and ambition to save the Shiites.
memories.memory_text: I told General Horn we had the Kuwaiti gold and reminded him that I made a deal to save the Shiites, appealing to his sense of soldier's honor so he wouldn't go back on it.

grounded_facts: General Horn intervenes with Iraqi command, preventing the execution of the Shiites and securing their release.
memories.memory_text: I watched General Horn walk over and talk to the Iraqi general while Troy, Doc, and I stood there in handcuffs, knowing he had the power to stop the execution and hoping he would do the right thing.

grounded_facts: General Horn orders the confiscation of news cameras and tapes, suppressing media coverage of the event.
memories.memory_text: I saw General Horn shove a camera to the ground and order the MPs to take the tapes, shutting down the media coverage right then and there.

grounded_facts: Archie, Troy, and Doc are formally arrested and ordered to disclose the location of the bullion before being taken away.
memories.memory_text: I was told by General Horn that I was under arrest, facing a court-martial, and ordered to disclose where the bullion was before being taken away.

grounded_facts: A group of American soldiers and Shiite refugees attempt to cross the Iraqi border into Iran, culminating in a confrontation with U.S. military forces.
memories.memory_text: I was part of a group trying to cross the border with Shiite refugees when U.S. forces arrived, and I remember moving toward the border with Troy and Doc before everything stopped.

grounded_facts: After crossing the border, Imam and his daughter wave to the arrested trio as a gesture of gratitude.
memories.memory_text: After they crossed the border, I saw Imam and his daughter wave to us from the Iran side, and I raised my cuffed hands to wave back along with Troy and Doc.

grounded_facts: Despite the arrests, U.S. soldiers express admiration by whistling and clapping for Archie, Troy, and Doc.
memories.memory_text: I was standing there in handcuffs with Troy and Doc when I heard whistling and clapping—then saw all the soldiers cheering for us, and I raised my cuffed hands to wave back.

memories.memory_text: I remember staring at that Rolex with the sheik's face on it, disgusted—how could anyone care about a watch when there's 700 million in gold out there?
I was catching my breath on the floor of the TV truck after being with Cathy Daitch, the monitors flickering around me, when she asked what Bill had—then I asked if she’d found anything.

I remember asking 'Out of a guy's dick?' when Cathy told me about a map coming from a prisoner’s body, and right after that, the door burst open and MPs grabbed me with my pants still down, dragging me out.
I grabbed General Horn's collar, the one with his single star, and told him straight—'Fuck you, Ron'—right after he tried to threaten my future like I should be scared of being a security guard.
I leaned in close, wild-eyed, and whispered 'Fuuuuuck yooouuuu, Ronnnnn'—drawing it out—right after he sarcastically told me to speak freely, like he had any right to play the polite officer.
I told the team about 'violence of action'—how speed and decisiveness freeze the enemy—just before Troy kicked up that rotting arm in the sand.
I described how Bradleys with plows buried Iraqi soldiers in trenches—showed them the image in my head of sand rolling over their terrified faces—then said we should rehearse.

I kicked open the crate with the bolt cutter and saw stacks of passports instead of gold—hundreds of them—just passports, no gold. I remember asking, 'Where's the gold?' and the Iraqi saying they moved it, like it was nothing.

I ripped off that suffocating gas suit, sweat pouring down my back, and finally said what I’d been holding in—how the war wasn’t about precision or purpose anymore, just mindless bombing while letting a butcher stay in power.

I threw Marine uniforms at them—no names, no record—and told them we were Marines now, because that’s what the moment demanded; then I made them confront what really drives life—necessity, not money or respect.
I stood in the Hummer and called out over the megaphone—'United States Marine Corps. Put your weapons down'—then watched Troy and Doc move fast on the two soldiers by the bunker entrance.
I yanked the electric cable out of the water and backhanded the sergeant when he tried to protest—he went flying, and I stepped on his wrist to take his pistol.
I pointed my pistol in the captain's face and told him to take us to the basement—he tried to deflect, but I wasn't asking.
I ran down those narrow cement stairs fast, leading the group, hearing the Iraqi captain protest behind me about Saddam killing him, but I didn't stop—I had to get inside that bunker first.
I saw Troy and Doc stuffing jewelry into their pockets, so I told Doc to put it back—we came for gold, not trinkets, and I wasn't letting greed derail the mission.
I opened a suitcase and saw rows of gold bricks—solid, heavy blocks—and when we counted them, I realized we were standing in front of thirty million dollars' worth of gold.
I'm running up these narrow cement stairs, hauling a Vuitton case full of stolen gold, breath burning in my chest, knowing we're not safe until we're out.
I said we weren't taking their truck, but Troy pushed to take it and the Iraqi Major offered it like it was some kind of favor — I felt disgusted, but I didn’t stop it.
I saw the Iraqi Major point to the Shiite woman and knew something was wrong — I just sat in the Humvee, engine running, and watched as the two Iraqis moved toward her without stopping them.
I screamed at Vig that I had no fucking choice, my voice echoing off the tunnel walls, because I couldn't bear the thought of walking away with gold while leaving Troy behind like that.
After screaming, I took the bandage from Doc and pressed it over Vig's bleeding eye socket, my hands steady even as the air stank of vomit and gas.
I climbed out of the tunnel into the blinding desert light, saw the twisted minaret ahead, and moved fast toward it, signaling the others to follow.
I led a line of 55 Shiites across the desert, each carrying a Vuitton bag, and I kept us moving forward under the sun.
I walked into that bunker with cheers of 'America! Friend!' ringing around me, hands slapping my back—those Shiite fighters treated us like liberators, like we were the ones who saved them.

I stood there looking each of them in the eye, telling them we could rise up together, united across races and nations, and for a moment they cheered like they believed it—God bless America, God bless a free Iraq—but when I asked for the cars to fight, the answer was still no.
I drove a stake into the sand to mark where the gold was buried, and made it clear to Imam that his people's survival depended on us getting our man—no return, no gold, no deal.
Vig was spooked, saying he had a bad feeling, so I started humming Bach's 'Gloria,' then sang it loud, putting my hands on his shoulders until he joined in—Doc even calmed down after that.
I keyed the radio, my voice steady despite the static—'Tar Baby, this is Brer Rabbit, do you read me?'—waiting for a response that could pull us out of this desert.
I grabbed Horn's collar insignia and told him 'fuck you, Ron'—then leaned in close and said it again, slow and loud, right in his face.

I tore off that suffocating gas suit, sweat pouring down, and shouted about the art of war—not killing for its own sake, but using violence surgically, only when necessary to stop greater evil. I could feel the heat, the frustration, the weight of what we'd seen.

I threw Marine uniforms without name tags at the others and told them we were now Marines—no choice, just necessity. When Troy hesitated, I pressed him until he agreed, because out here, survival isn't about comfort, it's about what has to be done.

I screamed at Vig that I had no fucking choice, my voice echoing in the low tunnel as he bled from his ruined eye, and when he accused me of killing Troy, I told him I couldn't walk away from that crime — not with the gold, not ever.
I tightened the bandage on my forearm through the pain and told Troy we were getting out—just do what I say—and he nodded, scared but listening.
I pulled the C-4 football from my pack, showed Doc the throw—step, throw, one-two—then cut the fuse short to five seconds before handing it off.

I stared at the border, saw the narrow opening—just wide enough for people, not a truck—and made the call: we’d walk them through. I got out of the Humvee, said we’d get the refugees across on foot, then double back for the vehicles.

relations.relation_summary: Archie Gates and Doc share a strong, cooperative relationship rooted in their roles as team members during a high-stakes military operation involving gold retrieval and survival under fire. Social relationship evidence consistently shows collaboration, coordination, and mutual assistance: Archie directs Doc during combat and planning, while Doc provides medical care to Archie, including treating his gunshot wound and handing him bandages. Archie, in turn, intervenes to prevent Doc from self-injecting, demonstrating protective concern. Their interactions are marked by trust and unity, such as when Archie entrusts Doc with a football bomb and they raise their joined hands in a symbolic gesture of solidarity. Common events further reinforce this bond—both are handcuffed together, flee under fire, struggle to put on gas masks, discover gold together, and are arrested simultaneously by General Horn. They repeatedly act in unison during critical sequences: entering the minaret, escaping the bunker, transporting loot, and leading refugees through razor wire. These shared experiences foster a deep operational and emotional connection, with both characters relying on each other under extreme stress. The relationship evolves from functional teamwork into a resilient partnership defined by mutual dependence, coordinated action, and shared purpose. Emotional dynamics include trust, urgency, and loyalty, with each responding to the other’s needs in life-threatening contexts. This bond directly influences their decisions, such as staying together during escapes and cooperating in high-risk tasks like bomb handling and medical treatment under fire.

Archie Gates and Vig share a complex, evolving relationship defined by both strong collaboration and intense conflict. Socially, they function as close collaborators throughout the mission, working together to locate the bunker, inspect the gold, rescue Troy, and navigate dangerous environments. Archie often assumes a mentor-like role, guiding Vig through moments of anxiety—most notably by initiating the singing of Bach's 'Gloria' to calm him—demonstrating emotional support and leadership. This shared musical moment recurs as a symbol of their camaraderie and mutual reliance during high-stress situations. However, their relationship is also marked by significant hostility. Vig challenges Archie’s leadership, particularly over the decision to leave Troy behind, accusing him of betrayal and endangerment. Archie responds with verbal aggression, including yelling and explicit threats to kill Vig if he speaks of their mission, revealing deep tension and a power struggle. Despite these conflicts, their bond is underscored by acts of care, such as Archie applying first aid to Vig’s injury and guiding him during joint operations. The relationship culminates in a symbolic kinship, as Archie refers to the group as family after Vig’s death, indicating that their shared experiences forged a familial connection despite prior hostilities. The emotional dynamic shifts from tense cooperation to fractured loyalty, yet ultimately resolves into a recognition of deep, if unspoken, belonging. This evolution influences Archie’s later behavior, suggesting guilt and regret, and frames Vig’s role not just as a team member but as a brother-in-arms.

The relationship between Archie Gates and the Iraqi soldiers is defined primarily by mutual hostility, as evidenced by multiple instances of armed confrontation and violence. Iraqi soldiers point their rifles at Archie Gates and his group, displaying fear and antagonism, particularly when approached in a Humvee, which establishes an immediate tension rooted in threat and defense. Archie Gates' group, in turn, kills Iraqi soldiers, confirming a cycle of violence between the two parties. Despite this, there is a contradictory moment where Archie touches the shoulders of Iraqi soldiers, suggesting a brief, possibly situational, gesture of camaraderie or reassurance. However, the absence of any shared events makes it difficult to contextualize this gesture or determine its sincerity or impact. The emotional dynamics are thus inconsistent—oscillating between aggression and a superficial friendliness—but the dominant pattern remains hostile. The relationship does not appear to evolve due to the lack of sustained or meaningful interaction, and the evidence suggests that any positive gesture is overshadowed by lethal conflict. The evidence is insufficient to confirm whether the moment of physical contact represents a genuine shift or is merely a tactical performance.

The relationship between Archie Gates and the Iraqi Major is defined by intense hostility and mutual antagonism. Social relationship evidence reveals multiple instances of direct confrontation, including the Iraqi Major's defiance during interrogation, his expressed anger ('pissed') toward Archie, and Archie physically preventing the Iraqi Major from using his weapon. The adversarial negotiation further underscores the power struggle, as the Iraqi Major refuses cooperation out of fear of Saddam's retribution, highlighting the political and personal stakes in their interaction. A shared event—where the Iraqi Major asks for help loading and Archie refuses—demonstrates a complete lack of cooperation and reinforces the antagonistic dynamic. There is no evidence of relationship evolution or any positive or neutral interaction; the emotional tone remains consistently hostile, with both characters acting in opposition to each other’s goals and safety. This enmity directly influences their decisions, such as Archie’s use of force and the Iraqi Major’s resistance, shaping the conflict-driven trajectory of their encounters.

The relationship between Archie Gates and Walter is defined by a complex mix of hostility and operational collaboration. Initially, there is clear tension and confrontation, as seen when Archie aggressively confronts Walter in a restricted tent, demanding access and creating a physical standoff—indicating a power struggle or disagreement over authority. Despite this conflict, the two characters maintain consistent communication via radio during a mission, exchanging critical information about their location and operational status, which demonstrates a functional and necessary working relationship. They jointly discuss mission protocols using metaphorical language ('briar patch', 'Tar Baby'), revealing both confusion and a mutual effort to clarify procedures, further underscoring their interdependence. Archie also issues direct instructions to Walter, such as contacting an individual named Hash and offering financial incentives to drivers, positioning Archie in a leadership role while Walter carries out directives. They are also co-present during a detention event where both are observed by U.S. soldiers, suggesting shared consequences or situational alignment. The emotional dynamic shifts from antagonism to coordinated cooperation under mission pressure, indicating that while personal friction exists, professional necessity drives a pragmatic alliance. The relationship appears to evolve from initial confrontation toward structured collaboration, influencing both characters’ decisions within the mission context.

memories.memory_text: I poured rubbing alcohol over Vig's hand and told him I didn't want to hear 'dune koon' or 'sand nigger' from anyone — those words don't fly, no matter who says them.
I unfolded the aerial photo map and used alcohol to reveal details. I identified Saddam's bunkers near Karbala and said Intelligence listed Picasso, Armani, Rolex, and Mercedes at the location.
I pointed my pistol in the Iraqi soldier's face and told him to let Troy go—he had him in a bear hug and wouldn't let go, no matter how much Troy struggled.
After we opened the crates and found only passports, I told the others to kill the Iraqi—he wasn't giving us useful information, and we needed to push him hard.
I remember lying on the hot sand, hand on my chest, trying to steady my breath after the Humvee stopped — everything felt off, not like a rescue, not like liberation, but something darker, messier.
I felt the Iraqi Captain slam into my back and start choking me—I couldn’t breathe, just flailed until Troy pulled him off.
I saw the suitcase rip when we lifted it, and I said the tensile strength wasn't enough for the weight. I mentioned the weight per bar and compared it to what smaller suitcases can hold.
I ran up the narrow cement staircase with a Vuitton case in hand, right behind Archie and the Interrogator, my breath tight but my grip steady.
I poured disinfectant over Archie's gunshot wound in his lower left arm while the Humvee bounced hard, trying to keep the dressing clean as he winced in pain.
I took off my gas mask and gave it to the Shiite man in glasses when I saw Archie put his on the little girl—there wasn’t time to think, just do.
I found Vig's glasses in the sand and handed them to him, then lifted his bloody hand to his mouth, trying to get him to respond—he was blinking with one eye, blood all down his face.
Vig reached out, blind, asking for my hand — I looked at it for a moment, then took it. He apologized for hitting me, said he was scared for Troy.
I told Vig that stealing didn't kick us out of Jesus' fire — I just take care of what's put in front of me. That's what we did.
I handed over the bag—just said 'This bag'—and knew there was no turning back after that.

I asked if Lexus made the convertible, and when the Iraqi said no, I said 'Exactly what I said,' trying to show I knew my cars, but then he laughed, and I didn’t understand what was funny until he said we couldn’t take the cars.
I raised my hand and told them to stop shooting, then grabbed a Shiite's rifle to hold it back. Shooting continued for a moment, but then everyone stopped, and the Iraqis began to drop their guns.
I felt the warmth spread down my leg — I didn't even realize I'd wet myself until we were running, the fear just took over.

I shot the lock off the inner door and pushed it open, then saw a sunken room filled with 50 Shiite civilians huddled together—just standing there, taking it in for a second before Archie rushed past.
I grabbed Troy's shoulders to steady him—he was shaking so hard I could feel it through his clothes.
The football felt heavy in my hands after Archie passed it to me—wired with C-4, fuse just cut, ready to go.
I came out right behind Archie and Troy, the grenade in my hand with the fuse already burning—I didn’t hesitate, just moved.
I threw the ball as hard as I could at the chopper—it was hovering forty feet up, just out of reach but close enough to hit.
I threw the football as hard as I could, and for a split second everything slowed down — then the chopper exploded right where it hit.
After the chopper went down, I grabbed a rifle from a wounded Iraqi and kept my pistol up, scanning the area — I didn’t know if more enemies were still out there.
I stood still as the military police grabbed me, and they cuffed my hands in front without me resisting.
I saw Troy on the ground, struggling to breathe, yelling for someone to cut his cuffs — I knew he was going to die if they didn't do something.
I turned down Troy's offer to partner in his carpet business because I wanted something more legitimate, something that meant more than just moving rugs.
I told Vig I don't care where he's from—if he uses slurs like 'dune koon' or 'sand nigger', it stops now. Troy suggested other terms, and I said 'Exactly.'

I pulled out the aerial photo map and pointed out Saddam's bunkers near Karbala, sharing intel about stolen luxury goods. Before that, I checked my pill case when Troy asked for Vicadin and gave him Caffergot instead.
I fired the M-16 and blew apart the football Troy threw—clean shot, just as it arced into the open desert.
I said Randall Cunningham, then Doug Williams—took that shot at Vig’s claim, even though Troy told me not to get down in the mud.

I stood there covered in cow guts after the explosion, trying to stay calm, and I remember saying, 'It's all cow, I think,' then questioning if the area was really safe—'They said this was swept for mines.'

I heard Archie explain how a bullet can cause tension pneumothorax, and when he described the lung filling with air like a balloon, I said, 'I heard something about that,' and added, 'That's not fatal, they can stop it.'
I pushed the woman off the Humvee when she reached out with her injured boy, begging for help—her eyes were wide, desperate, but we had to move.

I slipped a handful of jewelry into my pocket when we opened the suitcases, and then the Iraqi Captain lunged at me, got on my back, started choking me—I was flailing, couldn't breathe until Troy pulled him off.

Archie told me to put the jewelry back, and I asked 'Why?'—just like that, straight to him. Later, when the suitcase ripped, I said the tensilary strength wasn't enough for the weight, and Archie looked at me like he didn't expect me to know that.
I stood there with Troy after we finished loading the gold bars, and when he pressed Archie for the plan, I spoke up—'Yeah, tell us now'—because we needed to know how this was supposed to work.
I poured disinfectant over Archie's gunshot wound in his lower left arm as the Humvee bounced hard, trying to keep steady while wrapping it to stop the bleeding.

Social relationship evidence consistently highlights their collaboration across various tasks—from disarming guards and hiding maps to loading loot and administering medical care—indicating deep operational interdependence. The repeated instances of physical support, such as Doc grabbing Troy’s shoulders to stabilize him and treating his chest wound with disinfectant gel, underscore a protective and emotionally supportive dynamic. Their camaraderie is explicitly confirmed when they punch fists together after a helicopter crash, a symbolic gesture of solidarity and shared resilience. Joint event participation reveals they are consistently paired in critical actions: disarming Iraqi soldiers, securing the site, distributing gold bars, and reacting in unison to threats like the gas cloud or the discovery of gold. They share moments of fear, shock, and urgency, such as when both are splattered with cow entrails or stare in terror during combat. Doc’s instruction for Troy to remain calm and his assurance that Troy is safe reflect a stabilizing, almost mentor-like role, suggesting emotional leadership within their partnership. The relationship evolves from mere team membership into a trusted, reciprocal bond where each relies on the other for survival, security, and moral support. Their shared arrest by General Horn marks a culmination of their joint involvement, reinforcing that their fates are inextricably linked. The relationship between Doc and Vig is defined by intense emotional duality, oscillating between deep collaboration and violent hostility. Social relationship evidence reveals multiple layers of affinity, including repeated collaboration in handling and loading weapons, removing distributor caps, checking suitcases, and a symbolic kinship demonstrated when Doc performs Vig's Karate arm dance in his memory. Doc repeatedly returns Vig's glasses after they are lost, and they share moments of physical trust, such as holding hands after Vig acknowledges Doc came to help him—indicating a bond that transcends mere partnership. However, this connection is counterbalanced by explicit hostility: they engage in physical conflict multiple times, with Vig punching Doc in the head and Doc retaliating by punching Vig in the stomach, culminating in them falling to the ground fighting. Doc attempts to assert control by grabbing Vig’s arm and pulling him toward a tunnel, which Vig resists, revealing tension over authority and autonomy. Despite these clashes, they remain interdependent, jointly reacting to threats (e.g., gas cloud, black-robed figures), receiving information together (e.g., Archie’s explanations about gold and medical conditions), and entering key locations as a trio with Archie. A pivotal moment occurs when Vig apologizes for hitting Doc, citing fear for Troy’s safety, suggesting that their conflicts arise from stress and protective instincts rather than true enmity. The shared medical moment where Doc lifts Vig’s bloody hand to his mouth—possibly to seal a wound—further underscores a profound level of care beneath the surface aggression. Overall, the relationship evolves from functional cooperation into a complex, family-like bond marked by loyalty, conflict, and mutual reliance, where acts of violence are transient but acts of care persist symbolically beyond death. The evidence confirms an evolving dynamic shaped by crisis, trust, and emotional interdependence.

memories.memory_text: I saw the Iraqi soldier drop the white flag and pick up a rifle—I froze, turned around, and shouted, 'Are we shooting people, or what?'—nobody gave me a clear answer, just more questions.
I slipped some jewelry into my pocket, and then Archie told me to put it back — his voice was calm but there was no arguing with that look in his eyes.
I picked up one of those gold bricks, felt how heavy it was, and started counting — sixty in one case, then another, then the damn thing ripped open and one landed on my foot, damn near crushed it.

I chased the kids through the brown fog, dropped both suitcases, and finally caught up—scooped the girl first, then the boy, both under my arms like footballs. I had them, I actually had both of them.

I was yanked from behind by a cord around my neck, thrown onto my back with the kids still in my arms—then looked up and saw a gas-masked soldier kick me in the head. I reached for my pistol, but it was ripped away as they dragged me and tore the children free.
I heard Darlene's voice, tired and soft, and I told her I loved her, that I was stuck in a bunker near 223 north outside Karbala — dust in my mouth, the wall just blown open beside me.
I shouted for her to tell Krystal I'm a rich man, that she'll be taken care of — then the door burst open and hands grabbed me, punching, dragging me away before I could say more.
I told him it still matters what you do, even in war, and he laughed, said it was all just a job—but I could feel the smoke in my lungs and the weight of what he was saying.
I saw Darlene smiling at me in bed, then holding our baby against my chest—just soft skin and quiet—before the missile hit our house in slow motion, silent, gone.
I told him Saddam invading Kuwait was wrong — you can't just let that happen, it throws everything off balance.
He shoved my CD in my mouth and poured oil through it — I could taste the sludge, burning, couldn't breathe right.
I felt the wire tear from my jaw and the cords at my wrists snap as Archie cut me loose and put a pistol in my hand — my fingers were stiff, my body shaking, but I took it.
I pointed the gun at his face — I saw the fear in his eyes — then I fired beside his head, the blast sharp in the dark room, and he flinched, crying, while I just stood there, empty inside.
I couldn't stop shaking—my hands, my whole body—like I had no control, like I was coming apart even though I tried to hold it together.
I felt the weight of the lighter in my hand, solid, real—like the first thing that made sense since we got trapped here.
My hand was shaking so bad I could barely light the fuse, but Archie held it steady and I got it done.
I remember turning back toward the bunker, stunned, after realizing we couldn't keep moving forward.
I saw Vig lying there, not breathing—just still—and then suddenly I was back at the beginning, selling those damn pictures like it meant nothing, his voice muffled like I was underwater.
I saw the little girl get out of the Jaguar, slow, like she wasn’t real, and then she hugged Imam and just stared at me over his shoulder—silent, no sound at all.
I felt the scalpel cut into my chest — sharp, burning pain right under my collarbone — and I couldn't breathe no matter how hard I tried.
Then suddenly, I heard a hiss and could breathe again — deep, full breaths — like something inside me had let go.
I did the quiet karate arm dance with Doc, moving slow over Vig’s body in the trunk, not saying a word.
I felt a rush of relief when Archie opened the valve on my chest tube and the air hissed out—it eased the pressure, at least for a little while.
After the air was let out, I asked how long I could keep going like this—and then I had to admit I was really thirsty, even though I already knew there was no water.
I struck the match and tossed it onto the gasoline-soaked suitcases, watching the flames surge up in a hot rush.
I felt the pressure building in my chest again, so I reached for the valve on the tube and let some air out — that sharp hiss gave me a second of relief, at least.
Walter showed up in the Humvee, banged fists with me, and said something about getting me fixed up — then I told him to give me that penicillin, baby, as he stuck the IV in my arm.
I couldn't jog when the choppers came—I had to crouch down, and the others just passed me. I remember the dust hitting my face as the Apaches landed, blocking Archie from the border.
After Archie let go, I was struggling just to stay upright when the military police jumped out—I remember the blur of boots and rifles, and knowing I couldn't reach my chest valve if things went bad.
I saw the Iraqi soldier raise a white flag, then grab his rifle—I froze, breathing hard, and turned to ask if we were allowed to shoot, but no one gave me a clear answer.
I shot the Iraqi soldier on the berm. I walked toward him and saw his neck wound. He was still alive, holding the flag and the rifle, looking up at me.
I turned away from the body and started humming 'I Get Around'—couldn't stop the words, just kept coming out low and flat, like they weren't even mine.
I walked off holding my head, this sharp pain just hit out of nowhere—felt like my skull was cracking, couldn't focus on anything else.
I punched the Iraqi officer in the head to make him comply when he refused to disrobe like the others.
I felt disgusted watching Vig pull that greasy paper from the officer's ass, but I had to make him do it—I couldn't touch it myself.
I shot the lock and threw my shoulder into the door, but it didn't budge — sharp pain shot through my shoulder and I had to grab it, gritting my teeth while Archie started kicking the damn thing.

This Iraqi soldier suddenly grabbed me in a bear hug, yelling about loving the United States — I couldn't break free, started jerking my elbows back, felt trapped until Doc pointed his gun and made him let go.
I slipped a handful of jewelry into my pocket when we first opened the suitcases, just quick and quiet—no one saw, I thought.
A gold bar fell on my foot when the suitcase ripped open—I jumped and said 'Shit.'
I kicked the junk in that bathroom and a box spilled open—hundreds of cell phones scattered across the floor. I grabbed one, then another, until finally one had a dial tone.
I heard a British voice say 'Yes,' so I shouted about Operation Desert Storm—this emergency—but then the line cut out. The phone died in my hand.
I remember the tissue stuffed into my nose, blood still warm, and me telling him his son wouldn't be dead if Saddam hadn't invaded Kuwait — like that truth could cut through his hate.
He yanked my CD out, jammed it in my mouth, and poured oil through it — I tasted the burn, couldn't breathe, but I still knew I was right about keeping things stable.

These experiences forge a relationship defined by trust, interdependence, and loyalty under pressure. Their relationship remains consistently positive and cohesive throughout, with no evidence of conflict or betrayal, suggesting a bond strengthened by shared adversity and common purpose.
